Native engine book, chapter 5: inference

Source: vignettes/articles/native-book-5-inference.qmd

The first four chapters built the estimates. This chapter builds everything that comes with them: standard errors from the information matrix (expected and observed), standard errors of defined parameters (the delta method), robust standard errors for weighted data (the sandwich), the test of an indirect effect (MBCO), and the general likelihood-ratio test (anova()). Each is derived, computed by hand from the matrices of the earlier chapters, and checked against the engine and, where they offer the same quantity, against lavaan or OpenMx. The engine is experimental.

You need Chapters 1 to 4; the idea of a likelihood-ratio test
You get the covariance of the estimates from either information matrix and why the two differ, the delta method and the sandwich derived and rebuilt by hand, the MBCO test derived with its size argument, and anova() with its refusals
Time about 55 minutes 
library(medfit)

Attaching package: 'medfit'
The following object is masked from 'package:stats':

    decompose
library(generics)

Attaching package: 'generics'
The following objects are masked from 'package:base':

    as.difftime, as.factor, as.ordered, intersect, is.element, setdiff,
    setequal, union
rd <- function(x, d = 4) round(x, d)
d <- mediation_demo
n <- nrow(d)

# a well-fitting model: the usual mediation model, just identified (as many free parameters as
# moments, df = 0), so it reproduces the sample covariance exactly
full <- "
  mediator1 ~ a * treatment
  outcome ~ b * mediator1 + cp * treatment
  ab := a * b
"
# a badly fitting model: two mediators whose residuals are not allowed to correlate
parallel <- "
  mediator1 ~ treatment
  mediator2 ~ treatment
  outcome ~ mediator1 + mediator2
"

1. The covariance of the estimates

Maximum likelihood theory says that, in large samples, \(\hat\theta\) is approximately normal around the truth with covariance \(I(\theta)^{-1}\), where \(I\) is the information matrix of the log likelihood \(\ell\). Every standard error below is a square root of a diagonal entry of an estimate of that inverse. The engine’s discrepancy \(F_{ML}\) and the log likelihood are tied by \(\ell = -\tfrac n2 (F_{ML} + \text{constant})\) (Chapter 1), so

\[ -\nabla^2 \ell = \frac n2\, \nabla^2 F_{ML} . \]

There are two ways to turn \(I\) into a number you can compute from a fit.

Expected information

The expected information is \(I_E(\theta) = \operatorname{E}\bigl[-\nabla^2 \ell\bigr]\), the average of the curvature over repeated samples from the model. For the covariance part of the discrepancy it has a closed form; we derive it.

Step 1: the gradient. With \(S\) the sample covariance and \(W = \Sigma^{-1} - \Sigma^{-1} S\, \Sigma^{-1}\) (Chapter 1, without a mean structure), \(\partial_k F_{ML} = \operatorname{tr}(W\,\partial_k\Sigma)\).

Step 2: differentiate again. \(\partial_l\partial_k F_{ML} = \operatorname{tr}(\partial_l W\,\partial_k\Sigma) + \operatorname{tr}(W\,\partial_l\partial_k\Sigma)\), by the product rule.

Step 3: take the expectation. In large samples \(\operatorname{E}(S) \approx \Sigma\) when the model holds. Then \(\operatorname{E}(W) \approx \Sigma^{-1} - \Sigma^{-1}\Sigma\Sigma^{-1} = 0\), so the second trace, which carries the second derivative of \(\Sigma\) and is the hard part, vanishes. In the first, differentiating \(W\) gives \(\partial_l W = -\Sigma^{-1}\partial_l\Sigma\,\Sigma^{-1} + \Sigma^{-1}\partial_l\Sigma\,\Sigma^{-1} S\,\Sigma^{-1} + \Sigma^{-1} S\,\Sigma^{-1}\partial_l\Sigma\,\Sigma^{-1}\) (using \(\partial\Sigma^{-1} = -\Sigma^{-1}(\partial\Sigma)\Sigma^{-1}\)), which at \(S = \Sigma\) is \(\Sigma^{-1}\partial_l\Sigma\,\Sigma^{-1}\). So

\[ \operatorname{E}\bigl[\partial_l\partial_k F_{ML}\bigr] \approx \operatorname{tr}\bigl(\Sigma^{-1}\partial_l\Sigma\,\Sigma^{-1}\partial_k\Sigma\bigr), \qquad I_E = \frac n2 \operatorname{tr}\bigl(\Sigma^{-1}\partial_k\Sigma\,\Sigma^{-1}\partial_l\Sigma\bigr), \]

which is the covariance part of the formula of Chapter 1 (Section 8); with a mean structure the mean part \(n\,(\partial_k\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\partial_l\mu)\) is added. The engine evaluates it at \(\hat\theta\). Build it by hand for the badly fitting two-mediator model (no means, so only the covariance part) and compare:

fit_e <- fit_sem(parallel, d, information = "expected")
fit_o <- fit_sem(parallel, d, information = "observed")
ram <- fit_e@internals$ram
smp <- medfit:::.sem_sample(fit_e@data, ram)
theta <- fit_e@theta
sigma_inv <- solve(medfit:::.sem_implied(ram, theta))
dsig <- medfit:::.sem_dsigma(theta, ram)
q <- length(theta)
info_expected_by_hand <- 0.5 * n * outer(seq_len(q), seq_len(q), Vectorize(function(k, l) {
  sum(diag(sigma_inv %*% dsig[[k]] %*% sigma_inv %*% dsig[[l]]))
}))
info_expected <- medfit:::.sem_info_expected(theta, ram, smp, NULL)
c(difference = max(abs(info_expected_by_hand - info_expected)), largest_entry = max(abs(info_expected)))
   difference largest_entry
 2.842171e-13  3.200160e+03

Observed information

The observed information is the curvature of this one sample’s log likelihood at the estimate, \(I_O = -\nabla^2\ell(\hat\theta) = \tfrac n2\nabla^2 F_{ML}(\hat\theta)\). It needs no expectation and no assumption that the model holds. The engine computes the Hessian of \(F_{ML}\) by central differences of the analytic gradient: column \(j\) is

\[ \frac{\nabla F(\hat\theta + h_j e_j) - \nabla F(\hat\theta - h_j e_j)}{2 h_j}, \qquad h_j = \epsilon^{1/3}\max(|\hat\theta_j|, u_j), \]

with \(\epsilon\) the machine precision and \(u_j\) the parameter’s natural unit (Chapter 3), then symmetrizes the matrix and multiplies by \(n/2\). The step \(\epsilon^{1/3}\) balances truncation and rounding error of a central difference.

unit <- medfit:::.sem_step_floor(ram, smp)
h <- .Machine$double.eps^(1 / 3) * pmax(abs(theta), unit)
hess <- vapply(seq_len(q), function(j) {
  up <- dn <- theta
  up[j] <- up[j] + h[j]
  dn[j] <- dn[j] - h[j]
  (medfit:::.sem_grad(up, ram, smp) - medfit:::.sem_grad(dn, ram, smp)) / (2 * h[j])
}, numeric(q))
info_observed_by_hand <- n / 2 * (hess + t(hess)) / 2
info_observed <- medfit:::.sem_info_observed(theta, ram, smp, NULL)
c(difference = max(abs(info_observed_by_hand - info_observed)))
difference
         0

Why the two differ

Step 3 replaced \(S\) by \(\Sigma\), that is set \(W\) to zero, in two places: the second trace, and inside \(\partial_l W\). Keep \(S\) instead. Writing \(\Sigma^{-1} S \Sigma^{-1} = \Sigma^{-1} - W\) in the expression for \(\partial_l W\) gives \(\partial_l W = \Sigma^{-1}\partial_l\Sigma\,\Sigma^{-1} - \Sigma^{-1}\partial_l\Sigma\, W - W\,\partial_l\Sigma\,\Sigma^{-1}\), so the exact second derivative, times \(n/2\), differs from the expected information by

\[ I_O - I_E = \frac n2 \Bigl[\operatorname{tr}\bigl(W\,\partial_l\partial_k\Sigma\bigr) - \operatorname{tr}\bigl(\Sigma^{-1}\partial_l\Sigma\, W\, \partial_k\Sigma\bigr) - \operatorname{tr}\bigl(W\, \partial_l\Sigma\, \Sigma^{-1}\partial_k\Sigma\bigr)\Bigr]. \]

Every term is linear in \(W\), which is zero exactly when the model reproduces \(S\). So the better the model fits, the closer the two matrices. Check the formula on the badly fitting model, with the second derivatives of \(\Sigma\) taken by central differences of the engine’s analytic first derivatives:

w_mat <- sigma_inv - sigma_inv %*% smp$s %*% sigma_inv
h2 <- 1e-5
d2sig <- function(k, l) {
  up <- dn <- theta
  up[l] <- up[l] + h2
  dn[l] <- dn[l] - h2
  (medfit:::.sem_dsigma(up, ram)[[k]] - medfit:::.sem_dsigma(dn, ram)[[k]]) / (2 * h2)
}
gap_formula <- n / 2 * outer(seq_len(q), seq_len(q), Vectorize(function(k, l) {
  sum(diag(w_mat %*% d2sig(k, l))) - sum(diag(sigma_inv %*% dsig[[l]] %*% w_mat %*% dsig[[k]])) -
    sum(diag(w_mat %*% dsig[[l]] %*% sigma_inv %*% dsig[[k]]))
}))
gap_engine <- info_observed - info_expected
c(largest_entry_of_the_gap = max(abs(gap_engine)), formula_vs_engine = max(abs(gap_formula - gap_engine)))
largest_entry_of_the_gap        formula_vs_engine
            2.593267e+02             2.415070e-07

Now compare a model that fits exactly with one that fits badly. The mediation model is just identified: it has as many free parameters as moments (df = 0), so it reproduces \(S\) and \(W = 0\).

rel_diff <- function(text) {
  fe <- fit_sem(text, d, information = "expected")
  r <- fe@internals$ram
  s <- medfit:::.sem_sample(fe@data, r)
  ie <- medfit:::.sem_info_expected(fe@theta, r, s, NULL)
  io <- medfit:::.sem_info_observed(fe@theta, r, s, NULL)
  c(df = fe@df, chisq = fe@n_obs * fe@f, relative_difference_of_the_matrices = max(abs(io - ie)) / max(abs(ie)))
}
obs_exp <- rbind(`mediation model (just identified)` = rel_diff(full),
                 `two mediators, correlated errors omitted` = rel_diff(parallel))
obs_exp
                                         df         chisq
mediation model (just identified)         0 -3.552714e-13
two mediators, correlated errors omitted  2  1.382904e+02
                                         relative_difference_of_the_matrices
mediation model (just identified)                               5.898623e-09
two mediators, correlated errors omitted                        8.103554e-02

For the exactly fitting model the two information matrices agree to numerical precision; for the model that fits badly they differ by a visible fraction, and the standard errors follow:

se <- cbind(observed = sqrt(diag(fit_o@vcov)), expected = sqrt(diag(fit_e@vcov)))
se_ratio <- se[, "observed"] / se[, "expected"]
rd(cbind(se, ratio = se_ratio), 4)
                     observed expected  ratio
mediator1~treatment    0.1076   0.1076 1.0000
mediator2~treatment    0.1199   0.1199 1.0000
outcome~mediator1      0.0564   0.0472 1.1967
outcome~mediator2      0.0514   0.0430 1.1967
mediator1~~mediator1   0.0819   0.0819 1.0000
mediator2~~mediator2   0.1017   0.1017 1.0000
outcome~~outcome       0.0761   0.0761 1.0000
treatment~~treatment   0.0177   0.0177 1.0000

The two disagree only for the paths from the mediators to the outcome, the parameters the omitted residual correlation bears on. The engine’s default is the observed information (information = "observed"); the expected information is available with information = "expected".

Cross-checks

lavaan offers both. OpenMx computes its standard errors from a numerical Hessian, which corresponds to the observed information. Match the setting on each side:

lv_obs <- lavaan::sem(parallel, d, fixed.x = FALSE, information = "observed")
lv_exp <- lavaan::sem(parallel, d, fixed.x = FALSE, information = "expected")
nm <- names(theta)
c(observed_vs_lavaan = max(abs(sqrt(diag(fit_o@vcov)) - sqrt(diag(lavaan::vcov(lv_obs)))[nm])),
  expected_vs_lavaan = max(abs(sqrt(diag(fit_e@vcov)) - sqrt(diag(lavaan::vcov(lv_exp)))[nm])))
observed_vs_lavaan expected_vs_lavaan
      6.921905e-10       3.436773e-10 
suppressMessages(library(OpenMx))
mxOption(NULL, "Number of Threads", 1)
dat <- d[, c("mediator1", "mediator2", "treatment", "outcome")]
vars <- names(dat)
mod <- mxModel(
  "parallel", type = "RAM", manifestVars = vars,
  mxPath(from = "treatment", to = c("mediator1", "mediator2"), values = 0.4, labels = c("a1", "a2")),
  mxPath(from = c("mediator1", "mediator2"), to = "outcome", values = 0.5, labels = c("b1", "b2")),
  mxPath(from = vars, arrows = 2, values = 1, labels = paste0("v_", vars)),
  mxPath(from = "one", to = vars, values = 0, labels = paste0("m_", vars)),
  mxData(dat, type = "raw")
)
mx_pt <- summary(mxRun(mod, silent = TRUE))$parameters
se_mx <- stats::setNames(mx_pt$Std.Error, mx_pt$name)
map <- c("mediator1~treatment" = "a1", "mediator2~treatment" = "a2", "outcome~mediator1" = "b1",
         "outcome~mediator2" = "b2", "mediator1~~mediator1" = "v_mediator1", "mediator2~~mediator2" = "v_mediator2",
         "outcome~~outcome" = "v_outcome", "treatment~~treatment" = "v_treatment")
c(observed_vs_OpenMx = max(abs(sqrt(diag(fit_o@vcov))[names(map)] - se_mx[map])))
observed_vs_OpenMx
      6.725901e-06

The native engine’s observed standard errors agree with lavaan’s observed ones and OpenMx’s, and the expected ones with lavaan’s expected ones. The two kinds differ by the misfit term above, not by an error on either side.

2. Defined parameters: the delta method

A defined parameter such as ab := a * b is a function \(g(\theta)\) of the estimates. Its standard error comes from the delta method. Expand \(g\) around the truth to first order, \(g(\hat\theta) \approx g(\theta) + \nabla g^\top(\hat\theta - \theta)\). Then \(\operatorname{Var}\,g(\hat\theta) \approx \nabla g^\top V \nabla g\), because the variance of a linear function \(c^\top\hat\theta\) is \(c^\top V c\). For \(g = ab\) the gradient is \((b, a)\) in the two labels. The engine takes the gradient by central differences (step \(\epsilon^{1/3}\max(|x|, 1)\)); here the analytic one is easy:

fit <- fit_sem(full, d)
g <- c(coef(fit)[["b"]], coef(fit)[["a"]])
v_ab <- fit@vcov[c("a", "b"), c("a", "b")]
c(by_hand = sqrt(drop(t(g) %*% v_ab %*% g)), engine = fit@defined$se)
   by_hand     engine
0.08016376 0.08016376

The product \(ab\) is the indirect effect of the treatment on the outcome through the mediator, and its standard error is 0.0802.

3. The sandwich: robust standard errors

The inverse information is the right covariance only if the model, including the normal distribution, is correct and the data are unweighted. The sandwich estimator drops that assumption. We derive it in three steps.

Step 1: the estimating equation. Let \(s_i(\theta)\) be the score of row \(i\): the gradient of its (weighted) log density. The estimate solves \(\sum_i s_i(\hat\theta) = 0\).

Step 2: expand. Take a first-order Taylor expansion of the estimating equation around the truth \(\theta_0\): \(0 = \sum_i s_i(\hat\theta) \approx \sum_i s_i(\theta_0) + \bigl[\sum_i \nabla s_i(\theta_0)\bigr](\hat\theta - \theta_0)\). The bracket is the Hessian of the (weighted) log density summed over rows, \(-A\) with \(A\) the information (here \(A\) and \(B\) are the usual names for the sandwich’s bread and meat, not the RAM matrices). Solve: \(\hat\theta - \theta_0 \approx A^{-1}\sum_i s_i(\theta_0)\).

Step 3: the variance. The rows are independent, so \(\operatorname{Var}\bigl(\sum_i s_i\bigr) = \sum_i \operatorname{Var}(s_i)\), estimated by \(B = \sum_i s_i s_i^\top\) (each \(s_i\) has mean zero at the truth). Then

\[ V_{\text{sandwich}} = A^{-1} B\, A^{-1}. \]

When the model is correct and the weights are absent, \(B\) converges to \(A\) and the sandwich reduces to \(A^{-1}\).

The scores

For a covariance structure with the means unrelated to \(\theta\), row \(i\) has deviation \(r_i = x_i - \bar x\) from the (weighted) sample mean and score

\[ s_{i,k} = w_i\,\tfrac12\,\Bigl[(\Sigma^{-1} r_i)^\top \partial_k\Sigma\,(\Sigma^{-1} r_i) - \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1}\partial_k\Sigma)\Bigr], \]

with \(w_i\) the weight (1 when there are none). This is the derivative of the log density of Chapter 1 with respect to the covariance parameters (Section 8 of that chapter). With a mean structure the deviation is \(d_i = x_i - \mu(\theta)\), and the score gains the mean part \(w_i\,(\partial_k\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1} d_i\). Weights enter in two places: the weighted mean and covariance replace \(\bar x\) and \(S\) in the discrepancy, and the weights multiply the scores. The engine rescales the weights to sum to \(n\), so the result does not depend on their scale.

We build the sandwich by hand for a weighted fit and compare it with the engine. The weights are random, but fixed by a seed:

set.seed(4)
w <- rexp(n) + 0.3
fit_w <- fit_sem(full, d, weights = w, se_type = "sandwich")
ram_w <- fit_w@internals$ram
smp_w <- medfit:::.sem_sample(fit_w@data, ram_w, weights = w)
theta_w <- fit_w@theta

# Step 1: scores, built from the formula above
w_scaled <- w * n / sum(w)
sigma_w <- medfit:::.sem_implied(ram_w, theta_w)
sigma_w_inv <- solve(sigma_w)
dsig_w <- medfit:::.sem_dsigma(theta_w, ram_w)
r_mat <- sweep(as.matrix(fit_w@data[, ram_w$obs]), 2, colSums(w_scaled * as.matrix(fit_w@data[, ram_w$obs])) / n)
z <- r_mat %*% sigma_w_inv
scores <- vapply(seq_along(theta_w), function(k) {
  w_scaled * 0.5 * (rowSums((z %*% dsig_w[[k]]) * z) - sum(sigma_w_inv * dsig_w[[k]]))
}, numeric(n))
c(scores_by_hand_vs_engine = max(abs(scores - medfit:::.sem_scores(theta_w, ram_w, smp_w))),
  largest_column_sum = max(abs(colSums(scores))))
scores_by_hand_vs_engine       largest_column_sum
            8.881784e-15             1.594837e-07

The second number checks Step 1: the scores sum to zero at the estimate, which is the estimating equation.

# Steps 2 and 3: A^-1 B A^-1, with A the observed information of the weighted discrepancy
bread <- solve(medfit:::.sem_info_observed(theta_w, ram_w, smp_w, NULL))
meat <- crossprod(scores)
v_sandwich <- bread %*% meat %*% bread
model_based <- fit_sem(full, d, weights = w, se_type = "model")@vcov
medfit: `weights` supplied with `se_type = "model"`. Model-based standard errors are not valid under inverse-probability weighting; pass `se_type = "sandwich"` for robust (HC) SEs. (Shown once per session.)
c(sandwich_by_hand_vs_engine = max(abs(v_sandwich - fit_w@vcov)), largest_entry = max(abs(fit_w@vcov)))
sandwich_by_hand_vs_engine              largest_entry
              3.469447e-17               2.710643e-02 
rd(cbind(sandwich = sqrt(diag(fit_w@vcov)), model_based = sqrt(diag(model_based)))[1:5, ], 4)
                     sandwich model_based
a                      0.1548      0.1148
b                      0.0700      0.0492
cp                     0.1646      0.1157
mediator1~~mediator1   0.1274      0.0931
outcome~~outcome       0.1275      0.0903

The sandwich standard errors of the paths are larger than the model-based ones here: the weights vary, which the model-based formula ignores. (The last parameter, the variance of the binary treatment, is omitted from the table.)

With no mean structure, as here, the means are free and unrelated to \(\theta\): the information is block diagonal and only the \(\theta\) block of \(B\) enters. With a mean structure, the means are functions of \(\theta\) (Chapter 1), the scores carry the mean part, and the full information is used. The engine’s code handles the two cases in one function, so the check is to run both against lavaan’s robust standard errors with sampling weights:

dw <- d
dw$w <- w
fit_wm <- fit_sem(full, d, weights = w, se_type = "sandwich", meanstructure = TRUE)
lv_w <- suppressWarnings(lavaan::sem(full, dw, fixed.x = FALSE, sampling.weights = "w"))
lv_wm <- suppressWarnings(lavaan::sem(full, dw, fixed.x = FALSE, sampling.weights = "w", meanstructure = TRUE))
nm_w <- names(theta_w)
nm_wm <- names(fit_wm@theta)
c(covariance_structure = max(abs(sqrt(diag(fit_w@vcov)) - sqrt(diag(lavaan::vcov(lv_w)))[nm_w])),
  mean_structure = max(abs(sqrt(diag(fit_wm@vcov)) - sqrt(diag(lavaan::vcov(lv_wm)))[nm_wm])))
covariance_structure       mean_structure
        1.874922e-10         5.800585e-11

Without weights the sandwich is the Huber-White estimator. For a regression equation it equals the heteroskedasticity-consistent estimator HC0 (the one with no leverage correction), which gives something to check when the sandwich package is installed:

fit_u <- fit_sem(full, d, se_type = "sandwich")
eq1 <- stats::lm(mediator1 ~ treatment, d)
eq2 <- stats::lm(outcome ~ mediator1 + treatment, d)
hc0 <- c(a = sqrt(diag(sandwich::vcovHC(eq1, type = "HC0")))[["treatment"]],
         b = sqrt(diag(sandwich::vcovHC(eq2, type = "HC0")))[["mediator1"]],
         cp = sqrt(diag(sandwich::vcovHC(eq2, type = "HC0")))[["treatment"]])
rbind(HC0 = hc0, native_sandwich = sqrt(diag(fit_u@vcov))[c("a", "b", "cp")])
                        a          b        cp
HC0             0.1076145 0.05117436 0.1133901
native_sandwich 0.1076145 0.05117436 0.1133901

A weighted discrepancy is not a likelihood, so the quantities built on a likelihood are undefined for a weighted fit, and the engine refuses them:

say <- function(expr) {
  tryCatch({
    expr
    "no error"
  }, error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
}
restricted_w <- fit_sem(paste0(full, "a == 0\n"), d, weights = w, se_type = "sandwich")
msgs <- c(
  logLik = say(logLik(fit_w)),
  mbco_sem = say(mbco_sem(fit_w, "a", "b")),
  anova = say(anova(restricted_w, fit_w))
)
cat(sprintf("%s:\n  %s\n", names(msgs), msgs), sep = "\n")
logLik:
  logLik() is not defined for a fit with sampling weights: the weighted likelihood is a pseudo likelihood

mbco_sem:
  MBCO is not available for a fit with sampling weights: the weighted discrepancy is not a likelihood, so its difference is not chi-square.

anova:
  'restricted_w' was fitted with sampling weights: the weighted discrepancy is not a likelihood, so the difference of two of them is not chi-square.

4. MBCO: testing an indirect effect

The indirect effect \(ab\) is zero when either factor is. A test of \(H_0\colon ab = 0\) cannot use the usual delta-method \(z\): under \(H_0\) the gradient \((b, a)\) is zero when both are, so the standard error is zero there. MBCO (the minimum of likelihood-ratio tests, “model-based constrained optimization”) replaces it by a likelihood-ratio test per factor.

The statistics. Refit the model with \(a = 0\) and with \(b = 0\); each is a linear constraint (one solve, Chapter 3). With \(F\) the minimized discrepancy of the full model and \(n\) the number of rows,

\[ D_a = n\,(F_{a=0} - F), \qquad D_b = n\,(F_{b=0} - F), \qquad T = \min(D_a, D_b). \]

The null distribution. \(H_0\) is the union of two hypotheses, \(a = 0\) and \(b = 0\). Three cases, all asymptotic. If only \(a = 0\) is true, \(D_a\) is a likelihood-ratio statistic for a true restriction and has a \(\chi^2_1\) distribution, while \(D_b\) grows without bound with \(n\) (the restriction \(b = 0\) is false), so \(T = D_a \sim \chi^2_1\). Symmetrically if only \(b = 0\). If both are true, \(T \le D_a\) always, so \(P(T > c) \le P(D_a > c) = P(\chi^2_1 > c)\). In every case, \(P(T > c) \le P(\chi^2_1 > c)\): referring \(T\) to \(\chi^2_1\) gives a test whose size is at most the nominal level. It is conservative, and exactly right when one factor is zero and the other is not.

Why not solve \(ab = 0\) directly? The set where \(ab = 0\) holds is two lines, \(a = 0\) and \(b = 0\), that cross at \(a = b = 0\), where the constraint’s gradient \((b, a)\) vanishes. A local solver follows whichever branch is near its start and can stop on the worse one, and near the crossing it has no usable gradient at all. Chapter 3 showed the rule the engine uses instead: one linear fit per factor, keeping the one with the smaller discrepancy. That is exactly \(T\)’s smaller refit.

fit_full <- fit_sem(full, d)
mb <- mbco_sem(fit_full, "a", "b")
mb

    Minimum-of-two likelihood-ratio tests (MBCO) for an indirect effect

data:  a * b = 0
MBCO = 17.557, df = 1, p-value = 2.788e-05
refit_a <- fit_sem(paste0(full, "a == 0\n"), d)
refit_b <- fit_sem(paste0(full, "b == 0\n"), d)
by_hand <- c(D_a = n * (refit_a@f - fit_full@f), D_b = n * (refit_b@f - fit_full@f))
c(by_hand, T = min(by_hand), p_value = stats::pchisq(min(by_hand), df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE))
         D_a          D_b            T      p_value
1.755741e+01 1.620540e+02 1.755741e+01 2.787630e-05 
mb$tests
  constraint          f   diff_ll converged
1     a == 0 0.04389351  17.55741      TRUE
2     b == 0 0.40513506 162.05402      TRUE

The test table, the hand computation and the printed test agree: here \(D_a\) is the smaller, so the null that \(a = 0\) is the one the data come closest to, and \(T = D_a\). Two further checks. The engine’s rule for the constraint a*b == 0 fits the model once per factor and keeps the smaller discrepancy, so that is the smaller of the two refits:

fit_zero_product <- fit_sem(paste0(full, "a*b == 0\n"), d)
fit_zero_product@internals$branch
[1] "a == 0"
c(discrepancy = fit_zero_product@f, smaller_refit = min(refit_a@f, refit_b@f))
  discrepancy smaller_refit
   0.04389351    0.04389351

And lavaan and OpenMx give the same two likelihood-ratio statistics:

lv_full <- lavaan::sem(full, d, fixed.x = FALSE)
lv_a <- lavaan::sem(paste0(full, "a == 0\n"), d, fixed.x = FALSE)
lv_b <- lavaan::sem(paste0(full, "b == 0\n"), d, fixed.x = FALSE)

suppressMessages(library(OpenMx))
dat3 <- d[, c("mediator1", "treatment", "outcome")]
vars3 <- names(dat3)
mx_full <- function(fix_a = FALSE, fix_b = FALSE) {
  mxModel(
    "m", type = "RAM", manifestVars = vars3,
    mxPath(from = "treatment", to = "mediator1", values = if (fix_a) 0 else 0.4, free = !fix_a, labels = "a"),
    mxPath(from = "mediator1", to = "outcome", values = if (fix_b) 0 else 0.5, free = !fix_b, labels = "b"),
    mxPath(from = "treatment", to = "outcome", values = 0.2, labels = "cp"),
    mxPath(from = vars3, arrows = 2, values = 1, labels = paste0("v_", vars3)),
    mxPath(from = "one", to = vars3, values = 0, labels = paste0("m_", vars3)),
    mxData(dat3, type = "raw")
  )
}
m2ll <- function(m) summary(mxRun(m, silent = TRUE))$Minus2LogLikelihood
mx_stat <- c(a = m2ll(mx_full(fix_a = TRUE)) - m2ll(mx_full()), b = m2ll(mx_full(fix_b = TRUE)) - m2ll(mx_full()))
data.frame(
  test = c("a = 0", "b = 0"),
  medfit = mb$tests$diff_ll,
  lavaan = c(lavaan::fitMeasures(lv_a, "chisq") - lavaan::fitMeasures(lv_full, "chisq"),
             lavaan::fitMeasures(lv_b, "chisq") - lavaan::fitMeasures(lv_full, "chisq")),
  OpenMx = unname(mx_stat)
)
   test    medfit    lavaan    OpenMx
1 a = 0  17.55741  17.55741  17.55741
2 b = 0 162.05402 162.05402 162.05402

5. anova(): the general likelihood-ratio test

MBCO is a special case. For two fits to the same data, one a restriction of the other, the likelihood-ratio statistic is

\[ D = n\,(F_r - F_f), \qquad \text{df} = \text{df}_r - \text{df}_f, \qquad D \sim \chi^2_{\text{df}}\ \text{under the restriction}, \]

with \(F_f\) and \(F_r\) the minimized discrepancies and \(\text{df}\) each model’s degrees of freedom (which already count the equality constraints, Chapter 3). The reason: \(n F_{ML}\) is \(-2\log L\) up to a constant common to both models (Chapter 1), so \(D\) is \(-2\log\) of the likelihood ratio, Wilks’ statistic. anova() never refits: it compares the fits you give it, each fitted from its own start, so the statistic does not depend on where a refit would begin. With several fits it orders them by degrees of freedom and tests each against the previous one:

fit_a0 <- fit_sem(paste0(full, "a == 0\n"), d)
fit_a0b0 <- fit_sem(paste0(full, "a == 0\nb == 0\n"), d)
anova(fit_full, fit_a0, fit_a0b0)
Likelihood-ratio (chi-square difference) test for SEMFit models

n = 400; Chisq is n times the minimized discrepancy

         Df   Chisq Chisq diff Df diff Pr(>Chisq)
fit_full  0   0.000
fit_a0    1  17.557     17.557       1  2.788e-05 ***
fit_a0b0  2 179.611    162.054       1  < 2.2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
c(MBCO_D_a = mb$tests$diff_ll[1], anova_first_difference = anova(fit_a0, fit_full)$`Chisq diff`[2])
              MBCO_D_a anova_first_difference
              17.55741               17.55741

The first difference equals the first refit statistic of MBCO to every digit printed, and the second tests the b == 0 restriction added to a model that already has a == 0. The engine checks, before it computes anything, that the pair can be nested: the same observed variables and rows, more degrees of freedom for the restricted model, and no parameter freed in the restricted model that the other leaves out (parameter-table inclusion). These are necessary conditions, not a proof of nesting. Three refusals:

say <- function(expr) {
  tryCatch({
    expr
    "no error"
  }, error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
}
fit_more <- fit_sem("mediator1 ~ a * treatment\noutcome ~ b * mediator1 + cp * treatment + covariate1", d)
fit_b0 <- fit_sem(paste0(full, "b == 0\n"), d)
msgs <- c(
  `different variables` = say(anova(fit_a0, fit_more)),
  `same degrees of freedom` = say(anova(fit_a0, fit_b0)),
  `a single fit` = say(anova(fit_full))
)
cat(sprintf("%s:\n  %s\n", names(msgs), msgs), sep = "\n")
different variables:
  the models must use the same observed variables: fit_a0 (mediator1, outcome, treatment); fit_more (covariate1, mediator1, outcome, treatment)

same degrees of freedom:
  'fit_a0' and 'fit_b0' have the same degrees of freedom (1): neither restricts the other, so there is no likelihood-ratio test.

a single fit:
  anova() for a SEMFit needs at least two fits: the restricted model and the model it is nested in.

A fit where the data sit on the boundary of the parameter space gets a warning instead of an error. If a bound or an inequality on a tested parameter is active at the restricted fit (a > 0 together with the null a = 0), the null is on the boundary, the statistic is a mixture of chi-squares and not \(\chi^2_1\), and the p-value is not valid:

bounded <- fit_sem(paste0(full, "a > 0\n"), d)
bounded_null <- fit_sem(paste0(full, "a > 0\na == 0\n"), d)
boundary_warning <- tryCatch(anova(bounded_null, bounded), warning = function(w) conditionMessage(w))
boundary_warning
[1] "a bound on a is active at 'bounded_null': the null lies on the boundary of the parameter space, so the statistic is a mixture of chi-squares, not chi-square(df), and its p-value is not valid."

What the first five chapters built

Chapter The new object The check that can fail
1 \(A\), \(S_{\text{ram}}\), \(F\), \(m\); \(\mu\) and \(\Sigma\); \(F_{ML}\) and its gradient hand matrices against .sem_implied(), gradient against finite differences, logLik() against lavaan and OpenMx
2 the centered coordinates \(T\), \(c_0\) and \(V = T V_\phi T^\top\) standard errors unchanged under a shift of the data; lavaan and OpenMx fail where the engine does not
3 constraint rows, SLSQP, the gate, the Newton polish the gate rejects each planted bad solution; the polish matches a hand Newton iteration
4 fixed moments and the conditional likelihood equal estimates and standard errors; the cross block of the information is zero; logLik() against lavaan

Check yourself

  1. For which model is the observed information equal to the expected information at the estimate? (Answer: when the model reproduces the sample covariance, \(S = \Sigma\), the matrix \(W\) is zero and the dropped term vanishes: the just-identified model of Section 1.)
  2. Why does MBCO refer \(T = \min(D_a, D_b)\) to \(\chi^2_1\) and not to something with smaller critical values, since \(T \le D_a\)? (Answer: when only one factor is zero, \(T\) is asymptotically \(\chi^2_1\) itself, so smaller critical values would reject a true null too often.)
  3. A weighted fit has no logLik(). What would you need to compare two weighted models? (Answer: a likelihood; the weighted discrepancy is a pseudo-likelihood, so use a robust test built for it. The engine offers none and refuses the chi-square.)
